general.label: General
questions: Do you take on freelance or contract work?
answers: I am based in Mansoura, Egypt.
PHP and Laravel first, with MySQL and PostgreSQL. I also work in NestJS and Node.js, and I am comfortable with JavaScript.
Yes. I spent two years freelance before moving into full-time roles, and I still take the right engagement. Reach out via the contact page.

work.label: Work
questions: What kinds of teams do you work best with?
How do you approach performance work?
Do you lead, or do you prefer to be an individual contributor?
answers: Teams where product, frontend, and DevOps are in the decision, not handed a finished backend. The constraint has to be in the room while the scope can still move: what the user needs, what the client can render, and what production can actually run. That is how I work at Robusta, and how I led the backend team at Almasa.

I measure before I change anything. The cost is usually in the data path: the schema, the query, or an API that forces too much work onto the client. Indexes and cache come after that shape is right. I would rather fix the path than cache a bad query or hide it behind a spinner.

Both, and I do not treat them as different jobs. Leading is the technical decision, the scope, and the review, and it still includes writing the code that is easy to get wrong. I work that way now at Robusta. At Almasa I led a three-developer backend team the same way, and I still mentor.

process.label: Process
questions: How do you design an API?
What is your view on tests?
How do you use AI tools in the work?
answers: I design the contract before the routes: who calls it, which operations are allowed, what they can rely on, and how it fails. The resource model follows the domain, not the tables. Authentication and validation sit at the boundary, and anything outside the system stays behind an interface so the domain does not inherit a vendor's shape. A smaller API that can change without breaking clients beats a wide one that mirrors the database.
TDD where the behavior is easy to get wrong: permissions, payments, and query-heavy paths. I do not chase a coverage number.
I use them daily for implementation, tests, documentation, and debugging. They do not make the design decision, and I do not ship what I cannot explain. The architecture and the review stay mine.

about.title: Senior Backend Engineer.
about.subtitle: Seven years designing and delivering systems. The emphasis is a structure that holds up as the product grows.
intro: I am Ahmed. For seven years I have designed and delivered systems that other people keep running. I set the structure early, so the product can grow without the next change having to undo the last one.

That experience covers the whole system: how the parts fit, how the information is organized, and how the result stays maintainable once it is in use. I have led that work, and I have done it directly.

Communication is part of the same job. I explain the tradeoff in plain terms, agree the plan with the team, and keep the people who depend on the system clear about scope, progress, and risk. In code review I address the design as well as the change, and I write feedback that is specific, respectful, and clear about what to revise and why.

I hold the work to that standard. A system should remain sound after delivery, with a structure clear enough for the next change to follow. The people responsible for it should know the scope, the progress, and the risk, and they should be able to continue without reconstructing decisions that were already made.
